title: Arjuna asks: sit still or act?
hookLine: retreat or show up? on the battlefield, Arjuna asks which one is yoga
carry: karma yoga: evenness in action is yoga
tomorrow: a book full of poses says they're only stairs. to where?

cards: Two kinds of advice turn up in a hard season. Log off, go quiet, retreat. Or: get to work, show up, keep going.
On the field of Kurukshetra, with both armies waiting, Arjuna asks Krishna almost exactly this in the Bhagavad Gita. You praise giving up action, he says, and then you praise the yoga of action.
Tell me plainly which one is better.

teach.h: THE CASE FOR THE QUIET SEAT.
teach.b: Both answers have a home in the Gita. First, the case for sitting apart.
In chapter six, Krishna describes the yogi in a clean, quiet place, on a seat neither too high nor too low, body and head held steady, the mind gathered in.
And the tradition honors the sannyasin, who steps out of busy life altogether. Its best case: a scattered mind can't see clearly, so first you step out and get still.

Now the case for acting, which the Gita calls karma yoga, the yoga of action. In chapter two Krishna says samatvam yoga uchyate: evenness is called yoga. Stay the same in success and failure, and act.
Two verses later: yoga is skill in action. Its best case: life doesn't pause, and a stillness that only works in a quiet room isn't finished yet.

teach.h: BOTH LEAD TO THE HIGHEST GOOD.
teach.b: Krishna's own answer, in chapter five, is that both lead to the highest good, though of the two, the yoga of action is better. Then he adds that only the unwise speak of them as separate.
That's karma yoga, one of Hinduism's great paths: do your work fully, with an even mind, and offer it to God, whatever comes of it.

how: Hindu readers of the Gita find both paths in it: some take up sitting practice in a quiet place, as chapter six describes, and many offer their daily work to God as karma yoga, as chapters two, five and nine teach.

o: how yoga's practices and ideas traveled out from India
how Western teachers first carried yoga into India
how one yoga school spread by replacing all the others

games.q: two good cases. tap the pairs.
p: a quiet seat, the mind gathered in
the yoga of action, done evenly

s: the Gita only teaches yoga as action, never as sitting still
chapter six describes the yogi's quiet seat in detail.
in the Gita, Krishna calls yoga evenness
samatvam yoga uchyate: evenness is called yoga.
Krishna tells Arjuna that giving up action leads nowhere
he says both lead to the highest good, and prefers action of the two.

games.q: a friend is quitting social media for a month to 'get still.' you think it's running away. state her side's best case.
o: a scattered mind can't see clearly; stepping out first can help.
phones are bad, so anyone who quits is right.
she just wants attention for quitting.
games.why: the Gita gives the quiet seat a real place in chapter six. its best case isn't escape: a gathered mind sees more clearly.

practice: Pick one task waiting for you today: an essay, a shift, the dishes. In the Gita, Krishna asks that whatever you do be done as an offering to him, and many Hindus begin work that way. If you pray, offer the task silently now.
If you don't, set it before you as something you'll give full attention, whatever comes of it. Let the breath grow even, and stay.

wordCard.voice: Yoga's journey west: today through the Gita, where yoga is evenness, skill in action, and a quiet seat too.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Bhagavad Gita 2.48: evenness is called yoga.

carryVoice: Your line: karma yoga, evenness in action is yoga. On the mat and off it. Back tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 5.1–5.2 (Arjuna asks which is better, renunciation or the yoga of action; both lead to the highest good, the yoga of action excels)
Bhagavad Gita 5.4 (the unwise, not the wise, speak of sankhya and yoga as different)
Bhagavad Gita 6.10–6.13 (the yogi's seat in a clean place, neither too high nor too low; body and head steady; gaze toward the tip of the nose)
Bhagavad Gita 2.48 (samatvam yoga uchyate: evenness is called yoga) and 2.50 (yoga is skill in action)
Bhagavad Gita 9.27 (whatever you do, do it as an offering to me)
